content: The cardiotocograph, also referred to as an electronic fetal monitor (EFM), external fetal monitor, or non-stress test (NST), is a medical device used to monitor the condition of a pregnant woman, particularly during the third trimester. An ultrasound transducer is responsible for detecting and recording the fetal heartbeat. The cardiotocograph was developed by Dr. Orvan Hess and Dr. Edward Hon. When this device is used during the third trimester to assess fetal well-being, the procedure is referred to as a non-stress test (NST). A reactive non-stress test, which is considered a positive result, is defined by the fetal heart rate increasing (accelerating) by at least 15 beats per minute for a duration of at least 15 seconds, occurring at least twice within a 20-minute period. When the cardiotocograph is used during labor, the procedure is referred to as a stress test. Upon its introduction, the use of this device was anticipated to reduce the risk of fetal death during labor and to lower the incidence of cerebral palsy (CP). Over time, its use became nearly universal in hospital births across the United States. However, in recent years, there has been some debate regarding the effectiveness of the cardiotocograph in pregnancies that are considered low-risk. Critics argue that excessive reliance on this test may have contributed to an increase in misdiagnoses of fetal distress, which in turn has led to a rise in cesarean deliveries, some of which may be unnecessary.
